name: Mary Magdalene

seo.title: Saint Mary Magdalene: her life, the empty tomb and the myths
seo.description: Mary Magdalene in plain words: healed by Jesus, at His cross and His empty tomb, the first Easter news, why she was called a prostitute, and her feast.

band.lede: Jesus freed her from seven demons, and she followed Him to the cross. On Easter morning He called her by name, and she told the disciples, “I have seen the Lord!”

picture.alt: A painting by Jan van Scorel: Mary Magdalene, a young woman with golden-red hair braided and pinned up under a thin grey veil, sits beneath a tree and looks calmly out. On her lap she holds a tall golden jar of ointment. She wears a dark gown sewn with rows of pearls, its neckline lettered in gold, and a striped shawl. Behind her, pale rocky crags rise over a blue-green valley.
picture.credit: Mary Magdalene, Jan van Scorel, about 1530. Oil on wood. Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam. CC0.
picture.creator: Jan van Scorel

who: Mary Magdalene came from Magdala, a town on the Sea of Galilee. Jesus drove seven demons out of her, and she followed Him, helping to support His work. She stood near His cross and saw where He was buried. On Easter morning the risen Jesus called her by name, and sent her to tell His disciples.

tidbits.text: When the Gospels list the women around Jesus, her name comes first every time but once. At the cross in John, His mother is named first.
The English word **maudlin** comes from her name. Painters showed her weeping, so by about 1600 it meant tearful.
The *Golden Legend*, a medieval book of saints' lives, says the Lord made her “apostolesse of the apostles”.

cite.text: The Golden Legend, the Life of S. Mary Magdalene, tr. William Caxton (1483)

facts.label: In the Bible
facts.text: All four **Gospels** name her, **twelve** times in all, nearly always at the cross and the empty tomb. Luke alone names her before that, in Galilee.

facts.label: Her name
facts.text: **Magdalene** means from **Magdala**, a small town on the Sea of Galilee, between Capernaum and Tiberias. The town's name comes from the Aramaic for **tower**.

facts.label: Healed
facts.text: Jesus drove **seven demons** out of her, says Luke. The Gospels say nothing more about it.

facts.label: Family
facts.text: The Bible names no parents, **no husband** and no children.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Mary of Magdala**. **Myrrhbearer** and **Equal of the Apostles**, in the Orthodox Church. The **apostle of the apostles**, from Thomas Aquinas to a Vatican note of 2016.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: The Bible does not say. The Orthodox say she died at **Ephesus**, where John worked. A French legend puts her last years in a cave in **Provence**.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: A **jar of ointment**, for the spices she brought to anoint His body, as at the top of this page. The West long painted her as a weeping **penitent**, taking her for the sinful woman of Luke 7.

portrait.alt: A Greek icon on a gold ground: Mary Magdalene, with long auburn hair, sits beside an empty stone tomb with her hands clasped over her knees, looking up in sorrow. She wears a green dress under a red cloak. A golden jar of ointment stands on the tomb's lid. Pale rocks and a small tree rise behind her, and three little crosses stand on a hill at the left.
portrait.credit: Mary Magdalene, Konstantinos Tzanes, 1600s. Tempera on wood. Public domain.
portrait.creator: Konstantinos Tzanes
portrait.caption: Mary at the empty tomb, a Greek icon by Konstantinos Tzanes, 1600s. The three crosses of Golgotha stand behind her. Public domain.

gallery.alt: A painting by Piero di Cosimo: Mary Magdalene, a young woman with long wavy auburn hair threaded with pearls, sits at a stone ledge and looks down at a small open book. She wears a green dress with pale yellow sleeves and a red cloak lined with blue. A white lidded jar stands at the right, against a dark background.

west.text: **Mary Magdalene**, a **Catholic** feast since 2016, and a memorial before that. The **Church of England** keeps it as a Festival. The **Episcopal Church** keeps it too, and so do Lutherans in the **Missouri Synod** and the **ELCA**. The ELCA's calendar calls her Apostle.

east.text: **Myrrhbearer and Equal of the Apostles Mary Magdalene**, for the **OCA**. The Orthodox honour her again on the **Sunday of the Myrrh-bearing Women**, two weeks after Pascha.

feasts.note: Why 22 July? The book of martyrs of Bede, an English monk of the 700s, already names her on this day. Rome's calendar of 1969 notes that Syrian, Byzantine and Coptic Christians keep the same day, and that her feast spread in the West only in the 1100s. Churches on the old calendar keep 22 July 13 days later, on 4 August.

said.lede: The Fathers, and the medieval teachers who gave her a title, in their own words.

moments.title: Healed, and a follower
moments.text: Jesus went from town to town, preaching the good news of the kingdom of God. The Twelve were with Him, Luke says, “as well as some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities.” The first he names is “Mary called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out.” With Joanna, Susanna “and many others”, she supported them “out of their own means.”

moments.title: Near the cross
moments.text: On the night of His arrest, “everyone deserted Him and fled.” But the women who had followed Him from Galilee were there at His death. Mark names Mary Magdalene first among them. Matthew and Mark say the women were “watching from a distance”. John puts her “near the cross of Jesus”, beside His mother.

moments.title: Where they laid Him
moments.text: Joseph of Arimathea, a rich man and a disciple, took down the body of Jesus. He wrapped it in linen and laid it in his own new tomb, cut into the rock. Then he rolled a great stone across the entrance. “Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were sitting there opposite the tomb.” The women went home and prepared spices. Then they rested on the Sabbath.

moments.when: The first day of the week
moments.title: The stone rolled away
moments.text: When the Sabbath was over, she and two other women bought spices to anoint His body. They went at sunrise, wondering who would move the stone. It had been rolled away. Inside sat a young man dressed in white. “He has risen! He is not here!” In Matthew, Jesus Himself met the women as they ran to tell the disciples. They took hold of His feet and worshiped Him. Luke says that when they told the apostles, their words “seemed like nonsense to them”.

moments.title: Running to Peter
moments.text: John tells it through Mary alone. She came to the tomb while it was still dark, and saw that the stone had been removed. She ran to Simon Peter and the disciple Jesus loved, and told them the Lord had been taken. The two ran to the tomb and found only the linen cloths. “Then the disciples returned to their homes.”

moments.title: The gardener
moments.text: “But Mary stood outside the tomb weeping.” She bent down and saw two angels in white, sitting where the body of Jesus had lain. “Woman, why are you weeping?” they asked. She turned around and saw Jesus standing there, but did not know Him. He asked her the same question. Thinking He was the gardener, she asked Him where the body had been taken. Then Jesus said to her, “Mary.” She turned, and knew Him.

moments.title: Sent with the news
moments.text: “Do not cling to Me,” Jesus said, “for I have not yet ascended to the Father. But go and tell My brothers.” So Mary Magdalene went to the disciples with the news, and told them what He had said to her. The longer ending of Mark, missing from some early copies, says the same: “He appeared first to Mary Magdalene.” It adds that when they heard, “they did not believe it.”

words.note: Mary wrote nothing. These are her words as the Gospels record them. Outside the quiz's own section, every Bible line on this page is from the Berean Standard Bible.

feature.ctx: Jesus had just sent her to His brothers. She went to the disciples and told them what He had said to her.

extras.title: One woman, or three?
extras.lede: For almost fourteen centuries, most Christians in the West took Mary Magdalene to be the unnamed sinful woman of Luke 7, and Martha's sister Mary as well. The East never did. Here each side speaks for itself.

items.title: Three women in the Gospels
items.text: Luke 7 tells of “a sinful woman from that town”. At a Pharisee's dinner she wet Jesus' feet with her tears, wiped them with her hair and anointed them. Luke never gives her name. In his next chapter he names Mary Magdalene for the first time, among the women Jesus had healed. John tells of Mary of Bethany, Martha's sister, who anointed Jesus' feet days before His death. No Gospel says any two of them are the same woman. Jesus said of the woman in Luke 7:
items.quote: Therefore I tell you, her many sins have been forgiven, for she has loved much.

items.title: Gregory the Great: one woman
items.text: Pope Gregory preached on Luke 7 in Rome, in the church of St Clement, in about 591. He made the three women one. The seven demons, he said, meant “all the vices”. Her perfume was one she had once used on herself for forbidden deeds, and now she offered it to God. Most Latin writers followed him. As late as 1910, the *Catholic Encyclopedia* still argued for one woman: “To the Catholic mind it all seems fitting and natural.” Gregory's words, in our translation:
items.quote: She whom Luke calls a sinful woman, and John calls Mary, we believe to be the Mary from whom, Mark says, seven demons were cast out.

cite.text: Gregory the Great, Homilies on the Gospels, Homily 33; Catholic Encyclopedia, “St. Mary Magdalen”

items.title: The Orthodox: three women
items.text: “The Greek Fathers, as a whole, distinguish the three persons,” says the *Catholic Encyclopedia*, and the Orthodox still do. They keep Mary Magdalene on 22 July, and Martha's sister Mary with Martha on 4 June. The sinful woman is remembered in Holy Week: the hymns of Holy Wednesday, says the OCA, “remind us of the sinful woman who poured precious ointment on Christ's head at Simon the leper's house”. The OCA's life of Mary Magdalene does pass on a tradition that before Jesus healed her she “led a sinful life”. But it keeps her apart, and honours her as
items.quote: the woman called by the Lord Himself from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God.

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia, “St. Mary Magdalen”; OCA, Great and Holy Wednesday; OCA, Mary Magdalene, 22 July

items.title: Rome, 1969: three again
items.text: Many Protestant scholars already held that there were two or three women, the *Catholic Encyclopedia* noted in 1910. In 1969 Rome parted them too. Its new calendar kept 22 July for Mary Magdalene alone. Its notes are in Latin. Our translation:
items.quote: In the renewed Roman liturgy there will no longer be a memorial of Mary of Bethany, nor of the sinful woman of Luke 7:36-50, but only of Mary Magdalene, to whom Christ first appeared after His resurrection.

cite.text: Calendarium Romanum (1969), notes on 22 July; Catholic Encyclopedia, “St. Mary Magdalen”

myths.truth: No Gospel says so. Luke says only that seven demons had gone out of her. The idea came from joining her to the unnamed sinful woman of Luke 7, and Luke never calls that woman a prostitute either. Pope Gregory the Great joined them in a sermon of about 591, and the West followed him. The Orthodox never did, and Rome parted them again in 1969. See One woman, or three?, above.

cite.text: Luke 7:37; 8:2; Gregory the Great, Homily 33; Calendarium Romanum (1969)

myths.claim: Jesus would not let her touch Him.
myths.truth: He said, “Do not cling to Me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father.” Older English Bibles have “Touch me not”, and the Latin {la|Noli me tangere}, which became the name of countless paintings of the scene. In Matthew, the women “grasped His feet” and He did not stop them. Augustine found it absurd to think Jesus let the disciples touch Him “but refused it in the case of women”.

cite.text: John 20:17; Matthew 28:9; Augustine, Tractates on John, Tractate 121

myths.claim: She was the wife of Jesus.
myths.truth: No early writer says so. Some Gnostic books, written long after her time, made her the one who received His secret teaching, *Britannica* says. The *Gospel of Philip* is one. In 2012 Karen King, a Harvard scholar, announced a scrap of papyrus in which Jesus speaks of “my wife”. Scholars exposed it as a modern fake, and in 2016 King said the evidence “tips the balance towards forgery.” A medieval legend, *Britannica* adds, married Mary to John instead.

cite.text: Britannica, “Saint Mary Magdalene”; CNN, 13 September 2020, on Ariel Sabar's *Veritas*

myths.claim: The *Gospel of Mary* is her own lost Gospel.
myths.truth: It is not hers. It is a Gnostic book of the 100s, first written in Greek. The fullest copy is a Coptic translation, in a book of about 400 that was bought in Cairo in 1896 and published only in 1955. Two small Greek fragments survive too. Pages 1 to 6 and 11 to 14 are lost. In what is left, Mary tells the disciples what the Savior showed her. Andrew and Peter doubt her, and Levi takes her side.

cite.text: The Gnostic Society Library, notes on the Gospel of Mary; Britannica

myths.claim: She sailed to France and lived thirty years in a cave.
myths.truth: The Bible says nothing of her after Easter. The story is in the *Golden Legend*, compiled in the 1200s. With Lazarus, Martha and others, it says, she was “put in a ship in the sea, without any tackle or rudder, for to be drowned”, and came safe to Marseilles. Later she lived in a wild place “by the space of thirty years”, and at every hour of prayer angels lifted her into the air. The Orthodox tell a different later story: she preached in Rome, then went to Ephesus, where John worked, and died there.

cite.text: The Golden Legend, the Life of S. Mary Magdalene, tr. William Caxton (1483); OCA, 22 July; Catholic Encyclopedia

myths.claim: She gave the emperor the first Easter egg.
myths.truth: Not in the Bible. It is an Orthodox tradition. The OCA's life of her says she went to Rome and told the emperor Tiberius that Christ had risen. “According to Tradition, she brought him a red egg as a symbol of the Resurrection,” with the words “Christ is Risen!” The OCA credits her with the custom of giving eggs at Pascha.

circle.name: Mary of Nazareth
circle.text: Jesus' mother. John puts the two of them near the cross together.

circle.name: Peter
circle.text: She ran to tell him the tomb was empty, and he ran there to see. He went in and saw the linen cloths lying there.

circle.name: Martha of Bethany
circle.text: Not her sister, though the West long thought so. The Orthodox honour them both among the Myrrh-bearing Women.

cite.text: OCA, Sunday of the Holy Myrrhbearing Women

circle.name: The disciple Jesus loved
circle.text: He outran Peter to the tomb, went in, and “saw and believed.” The Orthodox say Mary ended her days near him, at Ephesus.

circle.name: Joanna
circle.text: The wife of Chuza, the manager of Herod's household. She helped to support Jesus with Mary, and went with her to the tomb.

circle.name: Mary the mother of James and Joses
circle.text: “The other Mary”, in Matthew. She sat with Mary Magdalene opposite the tomb, and went back with her at dawn.

circle.name: Salome
circle.text: At the cross with her, and one of the three women who bought spices to anoint His body.

circle.name: Joseph of Arimathea
circle.text: A rich man and a disciple. He laid the body of Jesus in his own new tomb while she watched.

circle.name: Jesus
circle.text: Her Teacher, Who freed her from seven demons. After He rose, He called her by name and sent her to His brothers.

saint.big: Yes. Every church that keeps saints' days honours her on 22 July. Since 2016 Rome has kept her day as a feast, the rank of the apostles' days.

churches.note: A Festival in the Church of England

paras: In 2016 Pope Francis raised her memorial to a feast. A Vatican note that year called her the first witness of the risen Christ and the first to tell the apostles. It gave her the old title of Rabanus Maurus and Thomas Aquinas: the apostle of the apostles.
The Orthodox call her Myrrhbearer and Equal of the Apostles. The ELCA's calendar names her “Mary Magdalene, Apostle”.
Rome's book of martyrs, in its 1916 edition, still placed her death at Marseilles, as the French legend has it:

quotes.q: At Marseilles, the birthday of St. Mary Magdalen, out of whom our Lord expelled seven demons, and who deserved to be the first to see the Saviour after He had risen from the dead.
